teaser: A portrait so startling that crowds followed its sitter around the exhibition.
review_notes:
Anecdotes (Grant followed by the crowd at the 1782 Royal Academy exhibition; the skating trip on the Serpentine and the cracking ice; 'below the fifth button'; Stuart 'lifted into fame by a single picture') come from early Stuart biographies (Dunlap, 1834) and NGA texts.
1878: shown in London attributed to Gainsborough; other names (Raeburn, Romney) were also proposed before Stuart's authorship was re-established.
Distant towers at left are identified by the NGA as Westminster Abbey.
Stuart calling his Washington copies 'hundred-dollar bills' is a traditional anecdote.
Size about 245 x 147 cm.

lesson.text: London, spring 1782. At the Royal Academy's yearly exhibition, visitors keep stopping in front of one tall canvas, then turning around to stare at a man in the room. “That is he, there is the gentleman!” The man is William Grant, a Scottish lawyer. The crowd trails him so closely that he ends up leaving.

What had they seen? A gentleman on ice skates. That sounds harmless now, but full-length portraits at the time were stately affairs: a figure standing still beside a column or a curtain, showing off rank. Nobody expected a man gliding straight toward them in the middle of his exercise.

The idea was an accident. Grant arrived for his sitting on a freezing day and remarked that it was better weather for skating than for posing. So painter and sitter went off to skate on the Serpentine, the lake in Hyde Park. The ice began to crack, and they retreated to the studio.

The painter was Gilbert Stuart, 26, an American from Rhode Island working as an assistant in London. He had a reputation for good heads and nothing else. Rivals joked that he could not paint a body “below the fifth button.” This picture, about 2.45 meters tall (8 feet), was his answer. Follow it from the hat down.

lesson.title: Below the fifth button
lesson.text: Four stops, top to bottom, on a figure painted almost entirely in black.

spots.title: A sideways glance
spots.text: Under the wide hat brim, cheeks flushed pink by the cold, Grant looks off to his right. He is watching where he is going, not posing for us.

spots.title: Crossed arms
spots.text: Arms folded high on the chest, one gloved hand showing. It is the pose of a skilled skater who needs no help with balance.

spots.title: Fur and linen
spots.text: A grey fur lapel and a white neckcloth are the only light notes on the body. They frame the face and stop the black coat from becoming a flat shape.

spots.title: Two blades
spots.text: One skate glides flat on the ice, the other trails behind on its edge. Silver buckles catch the light, and thin curved scratches on the ice record earlier turns.

lesson.text: Now you know why the crowd gasped. From the waist down this is the liveliest part of the picture: the legs cross, the coat tail swings out to the left, and the whole dark figure tilts very slightly. Stuart could paint below the fifth button after all.
A black figure against a grey sky is close to a silhouette. Stuart removes color so that the outline alone has to tell you about movement, and it does.

Grant is not alone on the ice. Stuart keeps the other people small and sketchy so they never compete with him, yet each little group is doing something specific. One of them has not even started skating.
Somewhere behind Grant, a man is still getting ready, bent over his feet. Can you spot him?

spots.title: Fastening his skates
spots.text: A man in a red coat crouches at the edge of the ice to strap on his blades. In the 1780s skates were tied onto ordinary shoes.

lesson.text: To his right, two friends lean against a bare tree and chat. On the left, skaters swing each other around by the hands. Far behind them rise the pale towers of Westminster Abbey. These clumsy, busy amateurs make Grant's calm look even more effortless.

For a while the painting lost its author. When Grant's family lent it to a London exhibition in 1878, it was shown as a work by the English painter Thomas Gainsborough. Stuart had left England so long before that few remembered his name.

He had left in a hurry. Success brought Stuart rich clients and richer habits, and by 1787 his debts drove him to Dublin, then in 1793 back to the United States. There he painted the most reproduced face in American history: George Washington, the portrait behind the one-dollar bill.
Stuart never finished that famous Washington head. Keeping it in his studio let him sell copy after copy for the rest of his life. He is said to have called them his “hundred-dollar bills.”

William Grant went back to being a lawyer, and history would have forgotten him. One cold morning and one good joke about the weather kept him gliding for more than two centuries. Since 1950 he has done it in Washington, in a city that did not exist when he laced up.

quiz.question: How did visitors react at the 1782 exhibition?
options: They followed the sitter around the room
quiz.explanation: People recognized William Grant and trailed him until he left.

quiz.question: What did rivals say Stuart could not paint?
quiz.explanation: He was known for heads only, until this full-length figure.

quiz.question: Where did Stuart and Grant go skating?
options: On the Serpentine in Hyde Park
quiz.explanation: They skated on the Serpentine before the ice began to crack.

quiz.question: What is the man in the red coat doing?
quiz.explanation: He crouches at the edge of the ice to strap on his blades.

quiz.question: To which painter was the portrait wrongly credited in 1878?
quiz.explanation: It was exhibited in London as a Gainsborough.

facts.text: Gilbert Stuart was an American working in London when he painted The Skater.
facts.explanation: He came from Rhode Island and was 26 at the time.

facts.text: Grant is dressed in bright red to stand out against the ice.
facts.explanation: He wears black; a small background figure wears the red coat.

facts.text: Stuart later painted the portrait of George Washington used for the one-dollar bill.
facts.explanation: He painted it after returning to the United States in 1793.
